Discrete-Time Signal
A discrete-time signal is a signal defined only at specific sampling instants, no longer a continuous function of time.<SEP>A Discrete-Time Signal is a type of signal referenced in the image caption as the result obtained from sampling the continuous-time analog signal.

Sampling
The process of measuring the amplitude of a signal at discrete, equally spaced points in time.<SEP>Sampling is the process of measuring the magnitude of a signal at discrete time points, converting a continuous-time signal into a discrete-time signal.<SEP>Sampling is a method for converting a continuous-time analog signal into a discrete-time signal, as introduced on Page 3 and further detailed on subsequent pages.<SEP>Sampling is the method or process described in the image caption for converting a continuous-time analog signal into a discrete-time signal.<SEP>Sampling is the process of taking discrete measurements of a continuous analog signal, which precedes the quantization step formalized by Equation 1.3.

Digital Signal
A signal represented by a sequence of numbers, each indicating the signal's amplitude at a specific sampling time.<SEP>A digital signal is a series of numbers representing the magnitudes of sampled values from a continuous signal after quantization.<SEP>A Digital Signal is a signal represented by a sequence of numbers, resulting from the analog-to-digital conversion process detailed in the document.

Binary Digit (Bit)
A binary digit (bit) is a digit in the binary system that can have a value of 0 or 1.

Analog Signal
A signal whose amplitude is continuous and analogous to the physical quantity it represents, processed by analog circuits.<SEP>A signal (v_A) that varies between 0V and +15V, represented by a digital word.<SEP>An analog signal is a signal where the amplitude at each sampling point can take any value within a continuous range.

Binary Number System
The binary number system uses digits 0 and 1, producing simple digital signals and circuits with two voltage levels.

Least Significant Bit (LSB)
The Least Significant Bit (LSB) is the bit with the smallest place value in a binary number.<SEP>The least significant bit (LSB) is the bit in the binary representation with the smallest weight, corresponding to b_0 in Equation 1.3.

Quantization
Quantization is the process of representing each sampled value with a finite set of numbers, making the signal amplitude discrete.<SEP>Quantization is a method that converts a discrete-time analog signal into a digital signal represented by a sequence of numbers, expected to be discussed on Page 4.<SEP>Quantization is the process of mapping a continuous amplitude to a finite set of discrete levels, formalized by the binary expansion in Equation 1.3.<SEP>Quantization is a key concept tested in Exercise 1.7, relating to the process of mapping analog signals to digital values.<SEP>A process discussed in the context of analog-to-digital conversion, mentioned as part of the foundational content preceding page 5.

Most Significant Bit (MSB)
The Most Significant Bit (MSB) is the bit with the largest place value in a binary number.<SEP>The most significant bit (MSB) is the bit in the binary representation with the largest weight, corresponding to b_{N-1} in Equation 1.3.

Quantization Error
Quantization error is the discrepancy between the original analog sample value and its digital representation.<SEP>Quantization error is a concept related to the process of converting analog signals to digital form, discussed on the preceding page.<SEP>Quantization error is the difference between the original analog value and its quantized digital representation, which is reduced by increasing the number of bits N.<SEP>Quantization error is the associated error from finite digital representation, which is calculated in sub-question (c) of Exercise 1.7.

Digital-To-Analog Converter (DAC)
A Digital-to-Analog Converter (DAC) is the dual circuit of an ADC, converting digital signals back to analog form.

Analog-To-Digital Converter (ADC)
An Analog-to-Digital Converter (ADC) is a circuit module that receives an analog input signal and outputs its corresponding N-bit digital representation.

Digital Circuit
A digital circuit is an electronic circuit designed to process binary digital signals.

Logic Circuit
A fundamental building block of digital systems, mentioned alongside storage circuits.<SEP>A logic circuit is a fundamental building block of digital systems that performs logical operations.

Digital Logic Inverter
The most basic digital circuit, introduced in Section 1.7.<SEP>A digital logic inverter is the most basic digital circuit, performing the logical NOT operation.

Analog Circuit
A type of circuit that can best implement certain signal processing functions.<SEP>An analog circuit is an electronic circuit that processes continuous analog signals.<SEP>Electronic circuits designed to process analog signals.

Memory Circuit
A memory circuit is a fundamental building block of digital systems used for storing information.

Figure 1.9
Figure 1.9 is a block diagram illustrating an Analog-to-Digital Converter (ADC).

Figure 1.7 (a)
Figure 1.7 (a) is an illustration of a continuous-time signal before sampling.

Figure 1.8
Figure 1.8 is an illustration showing a digital signal as a pulse train over time.

Figure 1.7 (b)
Figure 1.7 (b) is an illustration of a signal after sampling, showing its discrete-time nature.

Equation (1.3)
Equation (1.3) is the mathematical formula for representing an analog sample value as an N-bit binary number.<SEP>Equation (1.3) is a formula for binary encoding, specifically D = Σ (b_i * 2^i), which is required to solve the tasks in Exercise 1.7.

Digital Calculator
A digital calculator is an example of a device that uses digital signal processing.

Digital Watch
A digital watch is an example of a device that uses digital signal processing.

Digital Audio System
A digital audio system is an example of a device that uses digital signal processing.

Digital Television
Digital television is an example of a system that uses digital signal processing.

Digital Computer
The most important digital system, built from logic circuits and storage circuits.<SEP>The digital computer is the most important digital system, processing digital signals representing instructions.

Telephone Communication System
Telephone communication systems are traditional analog systems that have been largely digitized.

Signal
Information that is processed, amplified, and must be preserved without distortion.<SEP>A time-varying quantity that can be represented graphically, whose information content is conveyed by amplitude variations over time, contained in the "swings" of its waveform.<SEP>A time-varying quantity, such as voltage, that carries information and can be represented in either the time domain or the frequency domain.

Signal Processing Circuit
A circuit designed to perform specific functions on a particular signal, requiring a good description of the signal waveform for its design.

Signal Source Representation
Equivalent circuit models for a signal source, such as the voltage source and current source representations shown in Figure 1.1 (a) and (b).

Signal Waveform
The graphical representation of a signal's amplitude over time, which is often difficult to describe mathematically but is crucial for designing signal processing circuits.

Short-Circuit Current
The current that flows when the output terminals of a signal source are shorted together, denoted as i_sc.

Open-Circuit Voltage
The voltage observed at the output terminals of a signal source when no load is connected, denoted as ν_oc.

Source Resistance
The internal resistance of a signal source, denoted as R_s, which relates the source voltage ν_s and source current i_s.

Signal Spectrum
A highly useful description of a signal or any time function, representing it as a sum of sinusoidal components of different frequencies and magnitudes.<SEP>Signal Spectrum is the title of Section 1.2 and a key concept introduced under Chapter 1, relating to frequency domain analysis.<SEP>The signal spectrum is the graphical representation of the frequency components of an arbitrary waveform, as depicted in the image.

Fourier Series
A mathematical tool used to represent a periodic time function as an infinite sum of sinusoids whose frequencies are harmonically related.<SEP>Fourier Series is a mathematical concept introduced for analyzing signal spectra, specifically mentioned in the context of a square wave example.<SEP>Fourier Series is a mathematical tool referenced in the main text of the textbook.<SEP>Fourier series is a mathematical method for decomposing complex periodic signals into sums of sinusoidal components.<SEP>A mathematical method for representing a periodic function as a sum of sinusoidal components (sine and cosine waves) with different frequencies and amplitudes.<SEP>Fourier series are a method of signal analysis defined within the instructional material on Page 0 and Page 2.<SEP>Fourier series is a component of Fourier analysis mentioned in the technical discussions under Chapter 1.

Fourier Transform
A mathematical method used to analyze signals by transforming them from the time domain to the frequency domain, revealing their frequency spectrum.<SEP>A mathematical tool used to obtain the spectrum of a signal, applicable to both periodic and arbitrary time functions, providing a continuous frequency representation.<SEP>Fourier Transform is a mathematical concept mentioned as a potential new topic for continuation in Section 1.2 on Page 2.<SEP>Fourier transform is a mathematical method for representing non-periodic signals in the frequency domain.<SEP>A related mathematical method for representing aperiodic signals in the frequency domain, mentioned in contrast to the Fourier series used for periodic signals.<SEP>Fourier transform is a component of Fourier analysis mentioned in the technical discussions under Chapter 1.

Sinusoidal Signal
A signal of the form V_a sin(ωt), characterized by its peak amplitude V_a, angular frequency ω, and phase, crucial for circuit analysis, design, and testing.<SEP>Sinusoidal signal is a key concept introduced under the scope of Chapter 1.

Angular Frequency
The rate of oscillation of a sinusoidal signal in radians per second, denoted as ω, where ω = 2πf.<SEP>Angular frequency, denoted by $\omega$, is the rate of change of the phase angle in radians per second, related to frequency $f$ by $\omega = 2\pi f$.

Peak Amplitude
The maximum voltage or current value of a sinusoidal signal, denoted as V_a.<SEP>Peak amplitude, denoted by $V_a$, is the maximum voltage value in volts of a sinusoidal signal.

Frequency
The number of cycles per second of a periodic signal, measured in Hertz (Hz), denoted as f, where f = 1/T.

Period
The duration of one complete cycle of a periodic signal, measured in seconds, denoted as T.

Root Mean Square (rms) Value
A measure of the effective magnitude of a sinusoidal signal, equal to its peak amplitude divided by the square root of 2.

Fundamental Frequency
The lowest frequency component in the Fourier series representation of a periodic signal, denoted as ω_0, where ω_0 = 2π/T.

Symmetrical Square Wave
A periodic signal, such as the one shown in Figure 1.4, that can be represented by a Fourier series as an infinite sum of sinusoids at harmonic frequencies.

Phase
The initial angle of a sinusoidal signal at a reference time, determining its horizontal shift on a time axis.

Harmonic
A sinusoidal component in a Fourier series whose frequency is an integer multiple of the fundamental frequency.<SEP>A sinusoidal component of a periodic signal with a frequency that is an integer multiple of the fundamental frequency.

Figure 1.2
A figure showing an arbitrary signal waveform that is difficult to describe mathematically.<SEP>A figure describing a non-periodic time function, specifically a voltage signal v_a(t).<SEP>Figure 1.2 is a referenced figure that contains the original arbitrary waveform from which the signal spectrum is derived.

A circuit diagram showing a voltage source representation of a signal source.

Figure 1.1 (b)
A circuit diagram showing a current source representation of a signal source.

A figure illustrating a sinusoidal voltage signal ν_a(t) with peak V_a and angular frequency ω.<SEP>A labeled figure (Figure 1.3) depicting a sinusoidal voltage signal.

A figure showing the discrete frequency spectrum of a square wave signal.<SEP>A figure showing a spectrum, with the horizontal axis representing angular frequency ω in rad/s.<SEP>Figure 1.5 is a referenced figure that visualizes the frequency spectrum of a signal, likely displayed on Page 2.

Exercise 1.1
An exercise asking to determine the open-circuit voltage and short-circuit current for two equivalent signal source circuit representations and their parameter relationship.<SEP>Exercise 1.1 is a practice problem related to signal representation, located on Page 1 of the document.

Figure 1.6
A figure showing the continuous frequency spectrum of a non-periodic time function.<SEP>A figure showing the continuous frequency spectrum of a non-periodic signal.

Exercise 1.2
An exercise asking to calculate the source resistance given an open-circuit voltage of 10 mV and a short-circuit current of 10 μA.<SEP>Exercise 1.2 is a practice problem related to signal representation, located on Page 1 of the document.

ν_s(t)
The voltage of the signal source in the voltage source representation model.

i_s(t)
The current of the signal source in the current source representation model.

Equation 1.2
The Fourier series equation representing a symmetrical square wave signal as an infinite sum of sinusoids.<SEP>A mathematical equation representing the Fourier series expansion of a symmetric square wave signal, expressed as an infinite trigonometric series of sine functions with odd harmonics.

ν_a(t)
A sinusoidal voltage signal with peak amplitude V_a and angular frequency ω, as shown in Figure 1.3.

Storage Circuit
A fundamental building block of digital systems, mentioned alongside logic circuits.

Digital Signal Processing Technology
A widely used technology, though some signal processing functions are best implemented with analog circuits.

Electronic System
A system that often contains both analog and digital parts.

Electronic Engineer
A professional who must be skilled in designing analog circuits, digital circuits, and mixed-signal systems.

Mixed-Signal Design
Also known as mixed-mode design, it involves designing systems with both analog and digital parts.<SEP>This is a technical topic mentioned in the broader discussions connected to the textbook's foundational reference.

Amplifier
A fundamental signal processing function block used in almost every electronic system for signal amplification.<SEP>A fundamental signal processing function introduced in Section 1.4, characterized by its linearity requirement and defined input-output relationship.

Digital Word
A 4-bit word (D = b3 b2 b1 b0) used to represent an analog signal.

Transducer
A device that provides weak signals, necessitating amplification for reliable processing.<SEP>A device that converts a physical quantity into an electrical signal, often producing weak signals that require amplification.

Linear Requirement
A requirement for amplifiers to maintain the information in a signal without introducing new information or distortion.

Signal Amplification
The simplest signal processing task, required because transducers provide weak signals in millivolts or microvolts.

Distortion
An undesirable change in the waveform of a signal after amplification.

Amplifier Output Signal
The result of amplification, which should be an exact replica of the input signal but with a larger amplitude.

Exercise 1.7
An exercise involving the representation of an analog signal using a 4-bit digital word.<SEP>Exercise 1.7 is a pedagogical exercise located at the end of Section 1.3 on Page 5.<SEP>This is a detailed exercise on digital word representation mentioned as an example of the practical content within the textbook framework.<SEP>Exercise 1.7 is a structured, enumerated list of three sub-questions that form a pedagogical exercise on analog-to-digital conversion concepts.

Section 1.7
The section that introduces the digital logic inverter, the most basic digital circuit.

Periodic Signal
A signal that repeats its pattern over a fixed time interval, characterized by a discrete frequency spectrum including a fundamental frequency and its harmonics.

The Book
The text covers both logic and storage circuits, with the goal of training engineers in analog, digital, and mixed-signal design.

Non-Periodic Signal
A signal that does not repeat over time, characterized by a continuous frequency spectrum containing all possible frequencies.

Waveform
The shape of a signal; an amplifier must output a waveform that is a precise, scaled copy of the input waveform.

Spectrum
A representation of a signal in the frequency domain, showing the distribution of its amplitude or power across different frequencies.

Analog Video Signal
A signal with a frequency spectrum typically ranging from 0 MHz to 4.5 MHz.

Time-Domain Representation
A method of representing a signal by its amplitude as it varies over time.<SEP>Time-domain representation describes a signal as a function of time, such as $v_a(t)$.<SEP>A way of describing a signal by its amplitude as a function of time, showing the waveform's shape and behavior over time.<SEP>Time-domain representation is a method for representing signals, discussed as part of the technical content under Chapter 1.<SEP>Time-domain representation is a foundational concept for signal analysis discussed in the material preceding Page 3.

Sinusoidal Wave
A periodic wave characterized by its frequency (f) and angular frequency (ω), with examples given for calculating period (T) from frequency.

Square Wave
A periodic waveform described by a Fourier series, used in exercises to calculate power distribution among its harmonic components.<SEP>Square Wave is a type of signal used as an example in the discussion of frequency spectra and Fourier series analysis.<SEP>A square wave is an example of a complex periodic signal that can be decomposed into a sum of sinusoids via Fourier series.

Audio Band
The frequency range from approximately 20 Hz to 20 kHz, which encompasses the spectrum of sound signals like speech and music that are audible to the human ear.

Frequency-Domain Representation
A method of representing a signal by its frequency spectrum, such as V_a(ω) for a voltage signal v_a(t).<SEP>Frequency-domain representation describes a signal in terms of its frequency components, such as $V_a(\omega)$.<SEP>A way of describing a signal by its constituent sinusoidal frequencies and their amplitudes, showing the signal's spectrum.<SEP>Frequency-domain representation is a method for representing signals, discussed as part of the technical content under Chapter 1.<SEP>Frequency-domain representation is a foundational concept for signal analysis discussed in the material preceding Page 3.

UHF Television Broadcast Band
A frequency band from 470 MHz to 806 MHz, with each channel allocated 6 MHz, allowing for the calculation of the number of available channels.

Harmonic Frequencies
Frequencies that are integer multiples of a fundamental frequency (ω0), present in the spectrum of a periodic signal.

Angular Frequency ω
The rate of change of phase of a sinusoidal waveform, measured in radians per second (rad/s), used as the horizontal coordinate in spectral plots.<SEP>The angular frequency of the signal, calculated as ω = 2πf rad/s.

Figure 1.7
A figure illustrating the process of sampling an analog voltage signal to convert it into a digital signal.<SEP>Figure 1.7 is a potential figure that may appear on Page 3 or later in the document.<SEP>Figure 1.7 is a visual aid referenced on Page 3, illustrating the sampling process for converting analog signals to discrete-time signals.

Fundamental Frequency ω0
The lowest frequency component of a periodic signal, from which harmonic frequencies are derived.

Voltage Signal v_a(t)
An analog voltage signal used as an example, represented in both the time domain (as a waveform) and the frequency domain (as V_a(ω)).

Power P
The rate of energy dissipation, calculated for a square wave signal applied to a resistor using either direct integration or summation of harmonic contributions.

V_a(ω)
The frequency-domain representation (spectrum) of the voltage signal v_a(t).

Resistor
An electrical component to which a square wave signal is applied for power loss calculations.

Sampling Times t0, t1, t2...
Discrete, equally spaced points in time at which the amplitude of an analog signal is measured during the sampling process.

Digital Signal Processing
A digital watch is a practical application that implements digital signal processing technology.<SEP>Digital signal processing is the domain involving the analysis and manipulation of discrete signals, within which the binary conversion and quantization operate.<SEP>The domain of processing discrete-time digital signals, which contrasts with the continuous-time analog processing.

data.content: This equation represents a symmetric square wave voltage signal as an infinite sum of odd-harmonic sine waves with amplitudes inversely proportional to harmonic order. The decreasing harmonic amplitudes allow practical approximations by series truncation.

data.entity_name: Exercise 1.7: Application Problems on 4-bit Binary Representation of Analog Signals (list)
data.content: This is a three-part exercise list applying the theory of analog-to-digital conversion. It tasks the reader with: (a) converting specific analog voltages to 4-bit binary codes, (b) determining the analog voltage change corresponding to a toggle in each bit position (LSB to MSB), and (c) finding the digital representation for a fractional voltage and calculating the quantization error. Its purpose is to reinforce the preceding lesson on quantization, binary weighting, and ADC resolution within the chapter's foundational discussion on signal types.

This equation v_o(t) = A v_i(t) models an ideal linear amplifier's input-output relationship, where the output voltage is an exact scaled replica of the input voltage. It represents fundamental analog signal amplification without distortion, contrasting with the digital signal representation discussed earlier. The equation appears in the context of explaining how weak transducer signals are amplified for reliable processing in electronic systems.

Signal Source is a concept in electrical engineering with two equivalent representation methods.

Thevenin Form
Thevenin Form is one method for representing a signal source in circuit theory.

Norton Form
Norton Form is another method for representing a signal source in circuit theory.

Analog-To-Digital Conversion
It is a specific technical detail related to signal types, covered within the introductory chapter's material.<SEP>Analog-to-digital conversion is the theoretical concept being applied in Exercise 1.7, involving the binary representation of analog signals.<SEP>A foundational discussion on converting analog signals to digital form, including topics like quantization, which concludes on the preceding page of the document.
